reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / Fitzpatrick's Dermatology
clinicalPearls: A chronic, relapsing eruption of sterile pustules on the palms and soles that evolve through yellow pustules to brown macules and scaling on an erythematous, hyperkeratotic base
Lesions at different stages coexist, giving a characteristic mixed appearance of fresh pustules alongside older brown spots
Regarded by many as a localised variant of pustular psoriasis, though it has distinct associations and often occurs without typical plaque psoriasis
Very strongly associated with cigarette smoking, current or former, which is far more prevalent than in the general population, and it predominantly affects middle-aged women
Associated with thyroid disease and, within the SAPHO syndrome, with sterile osteoarticular inflammation, notably of the anterior chest wall
The pustules are sterile and culture-negative, an important distinction from infection
Often disabling because of fissuring, pain, and interference with walking and manual work, and it tends to resist treatment

Management includes smoking cessation, potent topical corticosteroids (often under occlusion), topical retinoids and vitamin D analogues, phototherapy, and systemic agents such as retinoids, methotrexate, ciclosporin, and biologics in severe disease
reference.pathophysiology: Palmoplantar pustulosis is an inflammatory disorder centred on the acrosyringium, the intra-epidermal portion of the sweat duct, of palmar and plantar skin, where accumulation of neutrophils forms the characteristic sterile pustules. It is thought to represent an autoinflammatory process with prominent innate immune involvement, including neutrophils and the interleukin-17 and interleukin-36 pathways. Nicotine and its effects on acrosyringeal sweat glands and immune signalling are strongly implicated, which fits the striking association with smoking, and the frequent overlap with psoriasis suggests shared inflammatory mechanisms.
additionalDifferentials: Tinea manuum or pedis with secondary pustulation
additionalInvestigations: Pustule swab and culture confirming sterility and excluding bacterial or fungal infection
Skin scrapings with potassium hydroxide microscopy and fungal culture to exclude tinea
Skin biopsy showing intra-epidermal neutrophilic (spongiform) pustules
Smoking history, given the strong association, with counselling on cessation
Thyroid function tests in view of the association with thyroid disease
Imaging (bone scan or MRI) and inflammatory markers if SAPHO syndrome or osteoarticular pain is suspected
redFlags: Bone or joint pain, especially of the anterior chest wall, suggesting SAPHO syndrome
Rapid generalisation with systemic upset raising concern for generalised pustular psoriasis
Severe fissuring with secondary bacterial infection
Disabling disease impairing walking or occupation and quality of life
reference.prognosis: Chronic and relapsing over years and often refractory to treatment; smoking cessation and appropriate therapy improve control, but complete and lasting clearance is difficult to achieve.
pitfalls: Repeatedly treating sterile pustulosis as a bacterial or fungal infection
Not addressing smoking, the strongest modifiable association
Underestimating the functional disability and its psychosocial impact
management: Smoking cessation as a key modifiable factor, with structured support
Potent topical corticosteroids, often under occlusion, combined with a topical vitamin D analogue and keratolytics as first-line therapy
Localised phototherapy such as hand-and-foot PUVA for resistant disease
Systemic agents for refractory cases including acitretin, methotrexate, ciclosporin or apremilast
Biologic therapy targeting the interleukin-17, interleukin-23 or interleukin-36 pathways in severe treatment-resistant disease
Screen for and manage associated thyroid disease
Assess for SAPHO syndrome with anterior chest wall pain and refer for rheumatological management if present
